graphInterpretation.stopExplanation: At t_apex = 0.506 s, the vertical velocity vy(t) crosses zero (vy = 0 m/s) as the basketball reaches its maximum height, but it does not stop completely in 2D space because its horizontal velocity remains constant at vx = 2.629 m/s.
graphInterpretation.accSignExplanation: Vertical acceleration ay = Δvy/Δt = -9.780 m/s² is negative across the entire flight [0.000 s, 1.000 s] because gravity pulls downward continuously while rising, at the apex, and while falling.

signedAreaValues.workSignedArea:
1) Slope of vy(t): ay = (vy2 - vy1)/(t2 - t1) = (-4.836 - 4.944)/(1.000 - 0.000) = -9.780 m/s².
2) Ascent Triangle Area₁ (+Δy_up on [0, 0.506 s]): ½(0.506 s)(4.944 m/s) = +1.250 m.
3) Descent Triangle Area₂ (Δy_down on [0.506 s, 1.000 s]): ½(1.000 - 0.506 s)(-4.836 m/s) = -1.195 m.
4) Net Displacement: Δy_total = +1.250 m + (-1.195 m) = +0.055 m.
5) Apex Height: y_max = y₀ + Δy_up = 1.200 m + 1.250 m = 2.450 m; Final Height: y_final = y₀ + Δy_total = 1.200 m + 0.055 m = 1.255 m.

studentWork.workRange:
Fundamental Equation: Δx = v₀x·t_hang + ½a_x·t_hang² (where a_x = 0 m/s²).
Substitution: Δx = (2.629 m/s)(1.000 s) + 0 = 2.629 m.
studentWork.workVector:
Launch Speed: v₀ = √(v₀x² + v₀y²) = √((2.629 m/s)² + (4.944 m/s)²) = √(6.912 + 24.443) = √31.355 = 5.600 m/s.
Launch Angle: θ = arctan(v₀y / v₀x) = arctan(4.944 / 2.629) = arctan(1.8806) = 62.00°.

state.reflectionText: Our video analysis of a basketball three-point shot confirmed that a projectile in free flight obeys the constant-acceleration kinematics model with remarkable precision. The experimental vertical acceleration obtained from the linear regression of our 10 two-point tangent slopes was ay = -9.780 m/s², yielding a percent difference of only -0.20% compared to the standard gravitational acceleration g = -9.800 m/s². Both the signed-area method under the vy(t) graph (Δy_up = +1.250 m above the time axis and Δy_down = -1.195 m below the time axis) and our algebraic kinematics derivation predicted an apex height of y_max = 2.450 m, matching the video measurement to within 0.00%. Furthermore, our interval analysis demonstrated a crucial physical concept: at t_apex = 0.506 s, the basketball stops moving vertically (vy = 0 m/s) as it transitions from rising to falling, yet it never stops moving in 2D space because its horizontal velocity remains constant at vx = 2.629 m/s and its vertical acceleration remains -9.780 m/s² downward across the entire [0.000 s, 1.000 s] flight. Minor experimental uncertainties in real-world sports video tracking arise from camera lens perspective distortion (parallax if the shooter is not strictly in the same plane as the 1.00 m calibration stick), slight motion blur of the basketball's center of mass at 60 FPS, and a small upward aerodynamic drag and Magnus backspin lift force. At a moderate launch speed of v₀ = 5.600 m/s, air resistance is small enough that horizontal acceleration remains effectively zero (ax = 0.000 m/s²). From a sports biomechanics perspective, releasing the basketball at a steep launch angle of θ = 62.00° increases the apex height (2.450 m) and steepens the entry angle into the hoop, giving the shooter a wider effective target opening than a flat trajectory.
